quests.hint: Try stressing every word in "out of stock" equally — it sounds stiff and unnatural, right? Which word loses its full vowel to fix that?
quests.explanation: English sentence rhythm relies on this kind of reduction — content words stay strong, function words like "of" go weak. That's why /ɒ/ becomes schwa in "out of stock".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "look" ends in a clear consonant sound, and "up" starts with a vowel. What happens to that consonant when you say them together naturally?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in a consonant meets a word starting with a vowel, the consonant shifts to open the next syllable instead of closing the first. In "look up", the final consonant of "look" links smoothly onto the vowel that begins "up".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try blending "freeze" straight into "yogurt" without a pause. The /z/ and /j/ fuse — into what sound?
quests.explanation: The two sounds don't just sit next to each other; they blend into /ʒ/. That's the defining feature of coalescence, and it's exactly what happens in "freeze yogurt".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Function words like "from" rarely keep their dictionary pronunciation in natural sentences. Listen for what its vowel becomes in "far from home".
quests.explanation: Because "from" isn't emphasized in "far from home", its vowel weakens from the full /ɒ/ to a fast, neutral schwa sound. This happens to almost every unstressed function word in fluent English.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.hint: In "I can do it", one word carries no stress at all. Focus on "can" — what happens to its vowel as a result?
quests.explanation: Weak forms like this one are what make native speech sound smooth rather than choppy. "can" trades its citation vowel /æ/ for schwa whenever it's unstressed, as it is in "I can do it".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.hint: "stop" ends and "pouring" begins with the exact same /p/ sound. Do you really hear it twice in natural speech, or just once?
quests.explanation: When the same consonant ends one word and begins the next, speakers don't pronounce it twice — they merge the two into a single, slightly longer sound. That's gemination, and it's exactly what happens with /p/ in "stop pouring".
quests.phoneticRule: When identical consonants meet at a word boundary, English merges them into a single, slightly longer sound instead of pronouncing both separately.

quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "just" get pronounced before "kidding", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "just" is the one that goes missing before "kidding".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "ten classes" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /n/ stay a /n/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /n/ ending "ten" turns into /ŋ/ because "classes" begins with a velar consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.explanation: Unlike linking, where the connecting sound is already written into the word, this /r/ in "opera every" comes from nowhere in the spelling. That's exactly what makes it intrusive rather than a genuine linking sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "remind" ends in /d/ and "yourself" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /d/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "remind yourself", /d/ + /j/ becomes /dʒ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.explanation: Say "as" on its own and you get the full vowel /æ/. Say it inside "as soon as possible" at natural speed, and it reduces to schwa — the standard weak form.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Vowel sounds rarely bump directly into each other in fluent English. What extra sound bridges "zoo" and "animals" here?
quests.explanation: Two vowel sounds meeting head-on is hard to say smoothly, so speakers add /w/ as a natural bridge. You'll hear it in "zoo animals", even though neither word's spelling contains it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "glass". What does that do to the /n/ just before it in "thin"?

quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.phoneticRule: Gemination avoids doubling identical adjacent consonants — the two collapse into one held sound rather than two short repetitions.
